channel.title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - All Critical Infrastructure
channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] The S7 advisory’s real finding: attackers are running AI-written exploitation scripts dressed up as OT monitoring tools
item.description: Joint advisory AA26-231A, published 19 August by NSA, CISA, the FBI, DOE and EPA, says threat actors are running AI-generated Python scripts — packaged to look like ordinary OT monitoring software — to find and reach Siemens S7 controllers across US critical infrastructure. The tooling is built on the snap7.dll and python-snap7 libraries and speaks S7comm, giving read and write access to PLC memory, configuration data and ladder logic. Targets are located through Censys and ZoomEye scanning, then reached through exposed interfaces, outdated firmware or weak authentication. S7-200, S7-300, S7-400, S7-1200 and S7-1500 are all named, across manufacturing, energy, water, chemical, food and agriculture. The agencies assess the activity as persistent reconnaissance positioning actors for later disruption, say the targeting is broader than Siemens, and state plainly that this is not a theoretical risk. - NSA / CISA / FBI / DOE / EPA joint advisory AA26-231A, building on AA26-097A — via CISA, BleepingComputer, Cybersecurity Dive - AA26-231A published 19 Aug 2026, re-verified this evening, 21 Aug 2026; AA26-097A published 7 Apr 2026, updated 22 Jul 2026; 12-state total through 14 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] Clop’s PLM extortion campaign now names Shell, GE and Philips — the stolen material is plant drawings and blueprints
item.description: Clop has listed 43 new victims tied to its exploitation of internet-exposed PTC Windchill and FlexPLM, the product lifecycle management platforms used across aerospace, defence, automotive, heavy machinery, medtech and retail. On 13 August Shell confirmed it is investigating a “potential incident” after the gang claimed 89 GB of data; on 17 August GE said it is assessing the claim and Philips confirmed a contained compromise of one enterprise server with no customer impact. The gang advertises backups, project plans, facility photographs, drawings, diagrams and blueprints. The entry point is CVE-2026-12569, an input-validation flaw in Windchill and FlexPLM exploited as a zero-day from early June for unauthenticated remote code execution and JSP web-shell deployment. On 18 August ReliaQuest published analysis of the implant itself, and it is not commodity tooling: a Java/JSP web shell written against Windchill’s own internal APIs, database schema, keystore and file-vault layout, with functions for credential access and decryption, repository enumeration, bulk file retrieval and arbitrary Java execution. It was engineered for PLM estates specifically. The detection problem is the part worth carrying into your own environment — the web shell runs as the application’s own service identity, so database telemetry can misattribute the activity as normal application behaviour, and query or file-access logs alone will not separate the theft from ordinary use. PTC began patching on 17 June; CISA added the flaw to KEV on 25 June with a three-day federal remediation deadline. No OT or control-system impact has been reported at any victim — this is confidentiality loss, not disruption. The OT relevance is what was taken: PLM holds the as-designed record of plants, machines and safety systems, and it is rarely inventoried as an OT-adjacent asset or covered by an OT threat model. - Clop leak-site listings and victim statements; implant analysis by ReliaQuest — via BleepingComputer, Computer Weekly - Victims named 14–17 Aug 2026; GE and Philips responses 17 Aug 2026; web-shell analysis published 18 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] An attacker crossed from a wind farm to a district heating plant through a shared private APN — and stopped a steam turbine
item.description: CERT Polska’s follow-up on the December 2025 Polish energy-sector intrusion, disclosed at DEF CON on 9 August and published on 11 August, describes what it calls the first observed case of an attacker reaching an OT network through a private cellular APN. The intruder compromised a FortiGate firewall at a wind farm, used a Teltonika cellular router on that network to enter a private APN operated by the distribution system operator, and from there reached a combined heat and power plant supplying roughly 50,000 residents — an entirely unrelated organisation. A steam turbine and the process-water treatment system were shut down, interrupting cogeneration. Operator response kept it to a short outage with no loss of heat supply. CERT Polska attributes the activity to a Russia-linked actor and notes the root cause was configuration, not exploitation: devices on the shared APN could reach each other freely, a pattern it found was common across Poland. - CERT Polska follow-up report — via SecurityWeek, BleepingComputer - Intrusion 29 Dec 2025; disclosed at DEF CON 9 Aug 2026, report published 11 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] CISA put the mass-exploited vCenter flaw in KEV today — and virtualisation is where OT lives now
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-59310 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 18 August, formalising what responders had been reporting for a fortnight. Broadcom published VMSA-2026-0006 on 29 July for the flaw, a directory-traversal issue in the vCenter syslog service rated CVSS 9.8 with no workaround. German incident-response firm QUIRSO observed the first victims connecting to attacker infrastructure on 3 August, five days later; by 5 August roughly 95% of an eventual 361 victim IP addresses across 47 countries had already appeared, concentrated in Germany, the US, Turkey, Iran and France. The actor gains root execution on vCenter, plants a cron job establishing reverse-SSH persistence, and in at least some cases deploys ransomware derived from leaked Babuk source. QUIRSO assesses with moderate confidence that the operator is Chinese-speaking, based on language artefacts in attacker scripts, tooling choices, victimology that excludes mainland China, and working hours consistent with UTC+08:00. No OT or industrial victim has been named. The relevance is structural: HMIs, historians, engineering workstations and SCADA servers increasingly run as guests, so root on vCenter is root on the plant’s supervisory layer. - CISA KEV catalogue; Broadcom VMSA-2026-0006 and QUIRSO campaign analysis — via BleepingComputer, Infosecurity Magazine - Patched 29 Jul 2026; exploitation from 3 Aug 2026; added to CISA KEV 18 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] All three North Carolina ports ran their gates by hand after a cyberattack — and the Coast Guard is still watching
item.description: The North Carolina State Ports Authority discovered an intrusion on 4 August and began recovery the following morning, activating its cybersecurity contingency plan across the Port of Wilmington, the Port of Morehead City and the Charlotte Inland Port. Gate openings were delayed and truck processing dropped to manual while the authority contained the intrusion; by 7 August a normal operating schedule had resumed with forensics continuing. The US Coast Guard confirmed it is monitoring the aftermath and coordinating with the North Carolina Department of Transportation, the state IT department and other federal partners. The authority has not disclosed the nature of the attack, which systems were hit, or whether vessel operations, cargo-handling equipment or rail interchange were touched, and no actor has been named — there is no reporting tying this to the Iranian-affiliated PLC campaign elsewhere on this page. Treat the OT question as open rather than answered: what is confirmed is enterprise and gate-management disruption, not control-system manipulation. Wilmington and Morehead City together move roughly 4.4 million short tons of bulk and breakbulk a year, much of it agricultural export, so the downstream exposure runs into food and agriculture supply chains as well as retail and raw materials. The transferable lesson is the one the authority got right: the fallback to manual gate processing existed, was documented and was exercised, which is why a multi-site IT compromise became a slow day instead of a closed port. - North Carolina State Ports Authority statements; US Coast Guard — via CyberScoop, The Record, BleepingComputer - Discovered 4 Aug 2026; recovery from 5 Aug 2026; Coast Guard confirmation and normal schedule restored 7 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] A chip-programming supplier pulled its own production and shipping systems offline to contain ransomware — and told the SEC it has no restoration date
item.description: Data I/O, the Redmond, Washington maker of the programming systems that load firmware onto automotive and consumer electronics, disclosed in an 8-K filed 21 August that it detected ransomware on 16 August. Containment meant taking systems offline, and the company states the outage reached internal and external communications, shipping, receiving, manufacturing production and other support functions. More than 65% of its business is automotive electronics programming, and it names Amazon, Apple, Google and Microsoft among its customers. As of the filing it could not offer a restoration timeline, and the scope and data impact remain under third-party investigation. No group has claimed the attack, no vector has been disclosed, and nothing published points to control-system compromise — which is precisely the pattern Dragos documented for the quarter and which is carried elsewhere on this board: production stops because the systems that schedule, route, program and document it stop. For anyone buying programmed microcontrollers, the exposure is a supply-chain one with two faces. The obvious face is delivery — a device programmer that cannot ship is a line-down risk for its customers. The less obvious face is code integrity: a firm whose function is writing firmware into parts you will install in your plant or product is a provenance dependency, and an intrusion at that firm is worth asking about explicitly rather than assuming was ruled out. - Data I/O Corporation Form 8-K filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission — via The Record, CyberScoop, SecurityWeek - Ransomware detected 16 Aug 2026; 8-K filed and disruption confirmed 21 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] Dragos counted 1,140 industrial ransomware victims in Q2 — and not one operator touched a control system
item.description: Dragos’ second-quarter industrial ransomware analysis records 1,140 victims, up 12% from 1,020 in Q1. Manufacturing absorbed 747 of them, 65% of the total; organisations supporting ICS environments accounted for 117 and transportation and logistics for 95. Qilin remained the most active brand, a position it has held since March 2025. The finding that matters for OT teams is the negative one: Dragos observed no ransomware operator directly manipulating an industrial control system during the quarter. Where production stopped, it stopped because enterprise IT was encrypted or because operators pre-emptively shut down virtualisation, identity or remote-access infrastructure that plant systems depended on. Social engineering — increasingly help-desk impersonation inside Microsoft Teams rather than email, walking staff through a screen-share to install remote-access tooling — was the most consistently reported initial-access theme. - Dragos Industrial Ransomware Analysis, Q2 2026 — via Help Net Security - Published 11 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] 4,407 Rockwell controllers answer from the public internet — and 22 sit in the exact towns being attacked
item.description: An internet-wide scan by Forescout Vedere Labs, published 6 August, found 4,407 internet-facing Rockwell Automation and Allen-Bradley programmable logic controllers: 65% in the United States, 12% in Canada, 3% in Spain. Twenty-two of them are in cities where water and wastewater utilities have reported cyberattacks since late July, and 19 of those 22 appear vulnerable to CVE-2017-16740, a buffer overflow in MicroLogix 1400 controllers that Rockwell patched nine years ago. Forescout’s central point reinforces the joint advisory: the effects described publicly — changed IP addresses, set passwords, lost visibility and control — needed no exploit at all, because the controllers were already reachable. Exposure has fallen 47% from a 2020 peak of 7,814, which is real progress and still leaves thousands of directly addressable controllers. - Forescout Vedere Labs — via The Hacker News, CyberScoop - Published 6 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] Refrigeration controllers can be switched off while the temperature display keeps reading normal
item.description: Claroty Team82 examined two supervisory controller platforms that run commercial and industrial refrigeration — Danfoss AK-SM 800A and Copeland XWEB Pro — and found serious flaws in both. In the Danfoss platform, three issues including an undocumented “code-of-the-day” authentication mechanism can be chained to bypass login and reach remote code execution. In Copeland’s XWEB Pro, Team82 reported 23 vulnerabilities, among them CVE-2026-25085, an authentication bypass in Lua-based middleware that exposes protected administrative API endpoints without credentials. The consequence researchers highlight is the one that defeats normal monitoring: an attacker with control of the supervisory unit can stop cooling while the operator display continues to report acceptable temperatures, so spoilage is discovered by inspection rather than by alarm. Danfoss shipped firmware R4.3.1 and Copeland firmware 1.13. This is coordinated disclosure — no exploitation has been reported. - Claroty Team82; Danfoss and Copeland advisories — via SecurityWeek - Reported 14 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] A CVSS 9.5 flaw in the FUXA SCADA/HMI platform lets an unauthenticated attacker write files to the server — scanning began within a day
item.category: Advisory — SCADA/HMI remote code execution, scanned in the wild
item.description: CVE-2026-25895 is a missing-authentication-plus-path-traversal flaw in FUXA, the open-source web-based SCADA/HMI package used for small automation projects, machine HMIs, remote monitoring and lab or pilot lines. In versions up to and including 1.2.9, a remote attacker with no credentials can write arbitrary files to the server file system and reach remote code execution — and because FUXA typically runs as the process front end, that is code execution on the box operators watch the plant through. VulnCheck reported broad internet scanning for the flaw beginning 18 August, from a single source address attempting to overwrite main.js with junk data; no working RCE payloads have been observed dropped yet, so treat this as reconnaissance ahead of exploitation rather than a confirmed compromise. Roughly 60 FUXA instances answer directly on the public internet. Two other FUXA flaws, CVE-2026-25939 and CVE-2023-33831, remain under active exploitation attempts, the latter with activity traced back to November 2025 and observed again this week — so this is a product already being hunted, not a one-off. Separately, watchTowr reported in-the-wild exploitation of CVE-2026-64849 (CVSS 9.3), an unauthenticated SSRF in the MLflow tracking server, used to pull cloud credentials from metadata endpoints; relevant if your analytics or predictive-maintenance stack runs MLflow alongside plant data. The uncomfortable part of the FUXA story is where these installs live: open-source HMI software rarely appears on an OT asset register, and the people who stood it up are often not the people who patch. - watchTowr and VulnCheck telemetry; vendor GitHub security advisories — via The Hacker News - CVE assigned 17 Aug 2026; scanning observed from 18 Aug 2026; reported 18 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] August ICS Patch Tuesday: a maximum-severity unauthenticated RCE in Siemens SIMATIC IoT2050, plus Schneider and Phoenix Contact fixes
item.description: Siemens ProductCERT published ten new advisories on 11 August. The one to act on first is SSA-834709: the Node-RED HTTP interface shipped on SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced devices running Industrial OS is missing authentication, so an unauthenticated remote attacker can create flows and execute arbitrary code on the underlying system with maximum privileges. Siemens rates it at the top of the scale and has released an updated version. A second critical code-execution flaw was fixed in Siveillance Video Management Servers. Schneider Electric published two advisories covering NetBotz 5 — two code and command execution issues — and PowerChute Serial Shutdown, where a missing limit on authentication attempts was corrected. Phoenix Contact also issued fixes in the same cycle. No exploitation of any of these has been reported. - Siemens ProductCERT SSA-834709, Schneider Electric, Phoenix Contact — via SecurityWeek - Published 11 Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] Haiwell’s IoT Cloud HMI gateway lets an unauthenticated attacker run OS commands as root
item.description: CISA advisory ICSA-26-225-02, published 13 August, describes an OS command injection flaw in the Haiwell IoT Cloud HMI Gateway. The Net Check feature reachable through the /setting endpoint passes user-supplied input to a cmdPing Socket.io event without sanitisation, so an attacker can inject and execute arbitrary operating-system commands with root privileges. Haiwell has released Scada-v3.50.1.19 to address it. The product is a cloud-connected HMI and remote-access gateway — the class of device that exists precisely to be reachable, which is what makes an unauthenticated root-command flaw in it worth treating as urgent even though no exploitation has been reported. Haiwell equipment is common in smaller integrator-built machine and process installations, where it is often commissioned once and never revisited. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-225-02 - Published 13 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] Six agencies warn Gunra is walking into critical infrastructure through two Fortinet bugs patched in 2025
item.description: CISA, the FBI, DC3, NSA, the US Secret Service and the Republic of Korea National Police Agency published joint advisory AA26-222A on 10 August, covering Gunra ransomware-as-a-service. The initial-access route is the part OT owners should read twice: Gunra affiliates are exploiting CVE-2024-55591 and CVE-2025-24472, two authentication-bypass flaws in Fortinet FortiOS and FortiProxy that grant super-admin privileges on the firewall. Both were patched in early 2025 and both are already in CISA’s KEV catalogue. Gunra emerged in April 2025, is written in C/C++ and is reportedly derived from leaked Conti source; it moved to a structured affiliate programme in early 2026 with a management panel, configurable builders and cross-platform payloads. The agencies count at least 51 victims across the Americas, Europe, the Middle East, Africa and Asia-Pacific, including hospitals, government bodies, financial institutions and critical manufacturing, with demands frequently above $10 million. Post-access tradecraft reported in the advisory includes abusing an SSL-VPN administrative account with default credentials and no lockout policy, OpenSSH tunnelling out to attacker infrastructure, and modifying authentication-processing files on a corporate VDI portal to permanently bypass MFA. Reconnaissance and lateral movement are deliberately scheduled between 22:00 and 06:00 local time. One victim lost tens of terabytes, staged through OneDrive and SharePoint before transfer to Mega. - CISA / FBI / DC3 / NSA / USSS / ROK National Police joint advisory AA26-222A — via The Record, Infosecurity Magazine - Published 10 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] Citrix is telling admins to patch NetScaler now — an unauthenticated bypass on the appliance that fronts most OT remote access
item.description: Citrix published a bulletin on 19 August covering two flaws in NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway, and followed it with an unusually direct instruction to upgrade immediately. The serious one is CVE-2026-19490, an authentication bypass a remote attacker can reach without credentials where the appliance runs as an AAA virtual server or as a Gateway — SSL VPN, ICA Proxy, CVPN or RDP Proxy — with exposure depending on firmware version and whether a SAML action is configured. The second, CVE-2026-19489, is a memory-overflow denial-of-service reachable when SIP ALG is enabled on a large-scale NAT group. Citrix has published configuration strings that let you check both preconditions from your own running config rather than guessing from version numbers: look for add authentication samlAction together with add authentication vserver or add vpn vserver for the first, and add lsn group.*sipalg for the second. Fixed builds are 14.1-73.32, 13.1-63.21, 14.1-73.32 FIPS and 13.1-37.277 FIPS/NDcPP. SecurAccess ZTNA Hybrid deployments running customer-managed NetScaler instances are in scope too. Neither flaw is reported as exploited yet, and neither is in KEV as of this edition — but the precedent is close and recent: Citrix issued the same kind of warning for CVE-2026-3055 on 23 March, attackers were abusing it within days, and CISA added it to KEV on 30 March with a three-day federal deadline. NetScaler has accumulated 22 KEV entries in five years, six of them used in ransomware. ShadowServer currently sees more than 22,000 NetScaler ADC and roughly 1,800 Gateway instances answering from the internet. For OT owners this is not an ICS advisory and it will not appear in an ICS feed, but it is the box that terminates integrator VPNs, vendor support sessions and engineering-workstation access into the plant — the same class of edge device that carried the intrusions in the Gunra and Polish district-heating cases elsewhere on this page. - Citrix security bulletin CTX696939 — via BleepingComputer - Bulletin published 19 Aug 2026; reported 20 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] Two TrueConf Server flaws are in KEV — and the attackers are swapping the client installers staff download from that server
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-72529 and CVE-2026-72530 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 20 August, with a three-day federal deadline on the first and two weeks on the second. TrueConf Server is self-hosted video-conferencing software, and the two flaws chain: the first is a missing authentication check that lets a remote attacker with access to TCP port 4307 call an undocumented function and run arbitrary scripts; the second breaks out of the isolated interpreter and executes on the underlying host. Together they are unauthenticated remote code execution on a server that normally sits inside the corporate network with broad reachability. CISA has not published exploitation detail, but Kaspersky’s ICS-CERT team reported on 12 August that the pair is being used by the Head Mare hacktivist group to deploy the PhantomCore backdoor. The chain Kaspersky describes: compromise the TrueConf server, replace one of its files with a web shell, use that to map the surrounding IT infrastructure and take privileged access to the TrueConf database, then — the step worth pausing on — replace the legitimate client installers hosted on that server, so employees who install the conferencing client get PhantomCore with it. Backdoors were also planted on the *nix hosts, one using the TrueConf protocol itself for command and control. Head Mare has been active since at least 2023, targeting organisations in Russia and Belarus in destructive rather than financially motivated attacks. Fixes shipped in June 2026 in TrueConf Server 5.3.9, 5.4.9 and 5.5.5 — every version since 2022 is affected — so this is a patch-gap problem, not a new flaw. The OT relevance is placement and blast radius rather than the product: conferencing servers are on-premises, often internet-reachable for remote workers, rarely owned by anyone in the OT programme, and frequently sit on a flat corporate segment with routes toward engineering workstations and the historian. A poisoned installer served from a trusted internal host is a supply-chain path onto engineering laptops that no amount of PLC hardening will catch. No OT or control-system impact has been reported. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue; exploitation analysis by Kaspersky ICS-CERT — via SecurityWeek - Fixes released Jun 2026; Kaspersky ICS-CERT report 12 Aug 2026; added to CISA KEV 20 Aug 2026, reported 21 Aug 2026

item.title: [Medium] NERC has to file the expanded internal network monitoring standard by 2 September, and it pulls EACMS and PACS into scope
item.description: SERC’s August compliance update sets out the CIP standards currently in flight, and one of them has a date close enough to plan around: NERC must submit a modified CIP-015-2 to FERC by 2 September 2026 extending internal network security monitoring to Electronic Access Control or Monitoring Systems and Physical Access Control Systems that sit outside the Electronic Security Perimeter. That is a meaningful widening. The first version of the standard concentrated monitoring inside the perimeter, and the systems being added — jump hosts, authentication and access-control infrastructure, badge and door controllers — are exactly the assets an attacker reaches first and the ones that grant onward access to everything else. The update also notes that CIP-003-9 became enforceable on 1 April 2026, that FERC approved the Virtualization Reliability Standards on 19 March 2026 — eleven modified CIP standards plus four new and eighteen modified glossary definitions — and that CIP-002-8 adopts a revised definition of “control center”. Registered entities that categorised assets under the old definitions should expect the scoping exercise to move. - SERC Reliability Corporation compliance update on approved and pending CIP standards; NERC and FERC filings - Update published 7 Aug 2026; NERC filing deadline 2 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] The Water Cyber Shield Act would give EPA mandatory-assessment authority and $300M a year for utility cybersecurity
item.description: Senators Klobuchar and Schiff introduced the Water Cyber Shield Act on 13 August, three weeks into the multistate PLC campaign. The bill would give EPA authority to require mandatory cybersecurity assessments of water and wastewater systems, direct $300 million a year through the Drinking Water and Clean Water State Revolving Funds for security improvements, and have EPA develop tiered standards in consultation with CISA, NIST, states and sector stakeholders, with additional flexibility and funding priority for smaller systems. It has been introduced, not enacted. - Sens. Klobuchar and Schiff — via WaterWorld, Wastewater Digest - Introduced 13 Aug 2026

item.title: [Medium] The information-sharing law that lets vendors warn you about OT threats expires at the end of September
item.description: The Operational Technology Cybersecurity Coalition — an industry group whose members include Forescout, Claroty, Dragos, Honeywell and Schneider Electric — issued a statement calling the water-sector attacks a wake-up call and pressing Congress and CISA on three items. The one with a date attached is the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015, whose liability protections are set to lapse at the end of September 2026. Those protections are the legal basis on which vendors, ISACs and operators pass indicators to CISA and on which CISA and the FBI push warnings back out to a wider set of potential victims — the mechanism that carried the PLC-campaign indicators to utilities that had not yet been hit. The coalition also asked CISA to issue a Binding Operational Directive covering operational technology at federal facilities (heating and cooling, power, physical access control), and asked Congress to reauthorise and fund the State and Local Cybersecurity Grant Program, the main funding route for the small municipal utilities in this campaign’s path. Coalition chair Alison King notes roughly 148,000 public water systems in the US, with only a small fraction participating directly in threat-intelligence sharing. - Operational Technology Cybersecurity Coalition statement — via Cybersecurity Dive - Statement 31 Jul 2026; reported 3 Aug 2026; CISA 2015 authority expires 30 Sep 2026
